articles.title: 7 de Setembro: veja FOTOS, VÍDEOS históricos e curiosidades do tradicional desfile em Brasília | G1
articles.standfirst: Ano após ano, Esplanada dos Ministérios se transforma em palco para tradição que atravessa gerações. Evento estreou em 1960 e reúne militares, estudantes, autoridades e famílias.
articles.summary: Ano após ano, Esplanada dos Ministérios se transforma em palco para tradição que atravessa gerações. Evento estreou em 1960 e reúne militares, estudantes, autoridades e famílias.
articles.body:
Segunda-feira, 7 de Setembro: dia do tradicional Desfile de Independência na área central de Brasília . Ano após ano, a Esplanada dos Ministérios se transforma em palco para uma tradição que atravessa gerações.

Realizado pela primeira vez em 1960, ano da inauguração da capital do país, o evento reúne militares, estudantes, autoridades e famílias. O g1 reuniu vídeos exclusivos do acervo da TV Globo com os desfiles ao longo das décadas (assista acima) .

Historiadores do Arquivo Público do DF também contaram curiosidades e fatos históricos sobre o desfile à reportagem.

"O desfile de 7 de Setembro é tradicional no Brasil inteiro, ele acontece em muitas cidades. Em Brasília, ele acontece desde o início e é um dos mais importantes do país, porque é onde está o chefe de Estado. É onde o presidente aparece e também é onde estão as Forças Armadas em maior presença", diz a historiadora Cecília Mombelli.

O primeiro desfile oficial de 7 de Setembro em Brasília foi realizado em 1960, com a presença do então presidente Juscelino Kubitschek.

Três anos antes, em 1957, a data foi celebrada em uma pequena comemoração para marcar o sentimento cívico que havia na população da época em relação ao país. Brasília, ainda não inaugurada, era um gigante canteiro de obras.

"Em 1958, a solenidade ficou um pouco maior, quando já contou com a participação do Exército, teve mais de 300 soldados, e também de 700 estudantes das escolas aqui da região", relata Cecília Mombelli.

O historiador Victor Hugo Tambelini explica que a celebração de 1958 representava que "Brasília já era uma realidade" e se tornaria, em breve, a capital da República.

"A parada de 1958, apesar de ter sido voltada para as pessoas que estavam aqui, para os trabalhadores, teve uma força muito grande justamente por mostrar que Brasília estava caminhando para esse lugar da inauguração", diz.

O sobrevoo de aviões da Força Aérea Brasileira (FAB) é um espetáculo à parte nos ares da capital. Sete aviões repetem movimentos sincronizados e, nos ares, riscam o azul do céu com fumaça.

A nuvem branca é gerada pelo contato do óleo quente com o ar. Sem poluir a atmosfera, as aeronaves deixam rastros geométricos que se desfazem em poucos segundos.

Segundo o superintendente do Arquivo Público do DF, Adalberto Scigliano, há relatos de que em 1960 os aviões teriam escrito JK nos céus em homenagem ao presidente.

Desde 1960, o desfile de 7 de Setembro é realizado todos os anos em Brasília . Os únicos dois anos em que não houve a celebração foram 2020 e 2021 , em razão da pandemia de Covid-19.

O ex-presidente da França, Nicolas Sarkozy, e o presidente do Brasil, Lula, em 7 de Setembro de 2009 — Foto: Reprodução/Wikimedia Commons

Adalberto Scigliano explica que outro fato curioso sobre o desfile de 7 de Setembro em Brasília é que ele já contou a presença de autoridades internacionais e celebridades.

"Autoridades como Christina Kirchner [ex-Presidente da Argentina] e Nicolás Sarkozy [ex-presidente da França]. Figuras midiáticas como Silvio Santos e Edir Macedo também já estiveram presentes", lembra.

Em todos os desfiles já realizados, uma figura nunca deixou de comparecer: a do presidente da República.

O desfile de 7 de Setembro na década de 60 — Foto: Arquivo Público do Distrito Federal

A historiadora Cecília Mombelli explica que o desfile de 7 de Setembro de 1961 teve uma simbologia muito importante.

"Naquele ano teve uma crise política, e aí o governo não era mais presidencialista, era parlamentarista. E também simbolizou a posse do presidente João Goulart, depois da deposição de Jânio Quadros, no dia 7 de setembro", diz.

Pedra Fundamental de Brasília, em Planaltina — Foto: Vinícius Melo/Agência Brasília

A Pedra Fundamental de Brasília , em Planaltina, foi erguida em 7 de setembro de 1922, há 103 anos , em comemoração ao centenário da Independência.

"O seu construtor recebeu a ordem para construí-la apenas 10 dias antes do dia 7 de setembro e, portanto, foi necessária a mobilização de cerca de 15 a 17 veículos, entre automóveis, caminhões e dezenas de pessoas para transportar as placas. A pedra começou a ser construída no dia 5 de setembro e foi concluída no dia 7, exatamente no dia de sua inauguração, às 12 horas", diz Adalberto Scigliano.

articles.title: ‘Preferi dormir em uma cadeira’: brasileiro deportado relata quatro dias detido em sala suja em Portugal | G1
articles.standfirst: Kauê Matos, de 19 anos, afirma que ficou sem tomar banho e passou os dois primeiros dias sem ver a família; jovem vivia no país havia dois anos com os pais e o irmão.
articles.summary: Kauê Matos, de 19 anos, afirma que ficou sem tomar banho e passou os dois primeiros dias sem ver a família; jovem vivia no país havia dois anos com os pais e o irmão.
articles.body:
Kauê Matos, de 19 anos, é deportado de Portugal após demora da AIMA em liberar documentação — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Antes de ser deportado de Portugal, o brasileiro Kauê Matos , de 19 anos, passou quatro dias detido em uma sala do aeroporto de Lisboa sem poder tomar banho e, nos dois primeiros dias, sem ver a família.

Em entrevista ao g1 , o estudante afirmou que o local cheirava mal, as cobertas estavam sujas e as camas, parecidas com macas de hospital, estavam em condições precárias. No primeiro dia, ele preferiu dormir sentado.

Kauê morava havia dois anos em Portugal com os pais e o irmão mais novo. No mês passado, ao retornar de um intercâmbio na Irlanda, foi impedido de entrar no país e levado para uma sala com outros imigrantes.

Segundo o jovem, eram servidas refeições durante o dia, mas não havia condições adequadas para tomar banho. Ele também afirma que os agentes não davam informações claras sobre o que aconteceria.

A comunicação com os pais era dificultada pela conexão ruim de internet no aeroporto. A mãe só conseguiu vê-lo pessoalmente dois dias depois da detenção.

Levado para avião e retirado antes da decolagem

Além da falta de informações, Kauê relata que recebeu orientações contraditórias durante o período em que permaneceu detido.

Em um dos dias, ele foi levado a um avião com destino ao Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos, em São Paulo. Segundo o estudante, somente depois de entrar na aeronave descobriu que seria deportado.

Antes da decolagem, no entanto, policiais o retiraram do avião e o levaram novamente para a sala de retenção. Os agentes disseram que a deportação não ocorreria mais.

Na última noite no aeroporto, Kauê acreditava que permaneceria detido por mais uma madrugada. Outros passageiros começaram a ser chamados para embarcar, mas o nome dele não havia sido anunciado.

Pouco antes das 23h, porém, agentes de imigração o chamaram e informaram que ele seria enviado ao Brasil.

Segundo o estudante, os policiais recolheram seu celular e seu passaporte, colocaram os itens em um envelope e disseram que ele só poderia recuperá-los após desembarcar em Guarulhos. Antes de entregar o aparelho, Kauê conseguiu enviar uma última mensagem aos pais, pedindo que tentassem impedir a deportação.

A família e o advogado afirmam que não foram avisados oficialmente sobre a deportação nem receberam informações sobre o voo. Um professor de Kauê identificou a aeronave e avisou parentes do estudante no Brasil para que fossem buscá-lo no aeroporto.

“Eu fico extremamente revoltado porque ninguém avisou os meus pais que eu estava sendo deportado”, afirmou.

A situação migratória de Kauê começou a se complicar em 2024, quando a família chegou a Portugal. Os pais deram entrada em pedidos de regularização por meio da chamada “manifestação de interesse”.

Esse mecanismo permitia que estrangeiros entrassem em Portugal como turistas e, depois de conseguir um contrato de trabalho ou iniciar uma atividade independente com contribuição para a Segurança Social, solicitassem autorização de residência.

Segundo a família, o processo, que deveria ser analisado em 90 dias, demorou dois anos.

Na época em que os pedidos foram apresentados, Kauê tinha 17 anos. A intenção era que, após a regularização dos pais, ele solicitasse autorização para viver no país por meio do reagrupamento familiar.

A decisão que autorizou a mãe a residir legalmente em Portugal saiu no começo deste ano. A do pai foi concedida no mesmo dia em que Kauê acabou detido no aeroporto.

Durante a espera, porém, o jovem completou 18 anos. De acordo com o advogado da família, Renato Teixeira, isso impediu que o caso dele fosse resolvido da maneira inicialmente planejada.

A alternativa seria solicitar uma autorização de residência como estudante, já que Kauê cursa o ensino médio em Portugal.

Segundo Renato, a legislação portuguesa prevê a concessão desse tipo de autorização. Para apresentar o pedido, no entanto, Kauê precisava acessar um formulário da Agência para a Integração, Migrações e Asilo (AIMA), que, de acordo com o advogado, não estava disponível no site do órgão.

A outra possibilidade seria agendar o atendimento por telefone, mas a família afirma que não conseguia contato com a agência.

“Você faz centenas e centenas de ligações, fica às vezes cinco horas tentando ligar para a AIMA e ninguém atende. Você envia e-mail pedindo agendamento e não tem resposta”, afirmou Renato.

Também seria possível ingressar na Justiça para obrigar a agência a realizar o atendimento, mas, naquele momento, a família não tinha condições financeiras de contratar um advogado.

Renato afirma que o problema atinge outros imigrantes, que acabam obrigados a recorrer à Justiça para ter acesso a procedimentos que deveriam estar disponíveis administrativamente.

Ao chegar ao Brasil, Kauê recebeu a notícia de que o processo que poderia permitir sua permanência em Portugal havia sido aceito.

“Se eu estivesse lá, era para eu estar na minha casa em Portugal neste momento, porque eles aceitaram. Se eu não tivesse sido deportado naquela hora, estaria livre na minha casa, com os meus pais e com o meu irmão”, disse.

O advogado estuda agora qual é o melhor caminho para que o estudante consiga retornar ao país. As aulas de Kauê recomeçam na segunda metade de setembro, e a família tenta evitar que ele perca o ano letivo.

Procurada, a AIMA afirmou que pedidos de nacionalidade ou cidadania são de responsabilidade do Instituto dos Registos e do Notariado (IRN) e que o controle das fronteiras cabe à Polícia de Segurança Pública (PSP).

"A AIMA esclarece que os pedidos de nacionalidade/cidadania são da competência do Instituto dos Registos e do Notariado. Por outro lado, o controle fronteiriço é da responsabilidade da Polícia de Segurança Pública, pelo que a AIMA não tem comentários a tecer sobre a alegada situação”, informou.

O Instituto dos Registos e do Notariado e a Polícia de Segurança Pública de Portugal também foram procurados pelo g1 , mas não responderam até a publicação desta reportagem.

articles.title: g1 20 anos: por que a cura do HIV ainda é um desafio para a ciência | G1
articles.standfirst: Após décadas de avanços no tratamento e na prevenção, pesquisadores tentam agora vencer um dos principais obstáculos à cura: o vírus que permanece escondido no organismo.
articles.summary: Casos raros mostram que eliminar ou controlar o vírus é possível. Pesquisadores agora tentam chegar a uma estratégia segura, duradoura e acessível.
articles.body:
Quarenta e cinco anos depois do início da epidemia de HIV, a ciência consegue falar de uma palavra que durante muito tempo pareceu distante: cura .

Ela ainda não existe como um tratamento simples e disponível para quem vive com o vírus. Mas já deixou de ser apenas uma possibilidade teórica . Segundo a Sociedade Internacional de AIDS (IAS, na sigla em inglês) , 13 pessoas são consideradas curadas do HIV — todas em situações muito específicas, principalmente após transplantes de células-tronco feitos para tratar cânceres graves .

O desafio agora é outro: conseguir o mesmo resultado sem depender de um transplante de medula, procedimento de alto risco que não é indicado para tratar o HIV .

No Brasil, uma das pesquisas que tentam chegar a esse objetivo é conduzida pelo infectologista Ricardo Diaz , professor da Universidade Federal de São Paulo (Unifesp).

“A gente está mais próximo agora. Então, é possível que a gente ainda consiga, nos próximos anos, observar alguma coisa diferente, que é a cura das pessoas sem precisar de um transplante de medula e começar a aumentar essa escala”, afirma Diaz.

Para entender por que isso ainda é tão difícil, é preciso olhar para uma característica do próprio HIV: a capacidade de se esconder dentro das células do organismo.

Registro de uma transmissão colorizada de numerosas partículas do vírus HIV replicando-se a partir de uma célula T. — Foto: NIAID

Os medicamentos antirretrovirais disponíveis hoje conseguem impedir que o HIV se multiplique e reduzir a quantidade de vírus no sangue a níveis indetectáveis.

Com o tratamento correto, uma pessoa pode ter boa qualidade de vida e chegar à carga viral indetectável , condição em que o HIV não é transmitido por via sexual.

O tratamento, porém, não elimina todo o vírus.

Parte do HIV permanece dentro de algumas células, principalmente do sistema de defesa, sem se multiplicar. Esses esconderijos são chamados de reservatórios virais .

➡️ Como o vírus está praticamente adormecido, os medicamentos não conseguem atingi-lo da mesma forma que combatem o HIV em atividade.

Por isso, quando o tratamento é interrompido, o vírus que estava escondido pode voltar a se multiplicar.

“O reservatório viral, que é a persistência do vírus, é o grande obstáculo para a cura”, explica Diaz.

Justamente por isso, eliminar ou controlar de forma permanente esse reservatório virou uma das principais frentes da pesquisa mundial sobre cura do HIV.

Células CD4 infectadas pelo HIV passam a ser usadas pelo vírus para produzir novas cópias. — Foto: Reprodução/AboutKidsHealth.ca

Os casos já registrados de cura mostraram que eliminar o HIV do organismo é possível. O primeiro deles foi o americano Timothy Ray Brown , conhecido como “ paciente de Berlim ”.

Ele e os demais pacientes curados precisavam de transplantes para tratar doenças graves, como leucemia ou linfoma. Em alguns desses casos, os doadores tinham uma alteração genética que dificulta a entrada do HIV nas células.

O transplante também substitui grande parte das células do sistema imunológico e pode ajudar a eliminar células que ainda carregavam o vírus.

Mas esse caminho não pode ser reproduzido simplesmente em milhões de pessoas com HIV. O transplante traz riscos importantes e só se justifica quando há outra doença grave que exige o procedimento.

Por isso, os pesquisadores tentam descobrir quais mecanismos levaram à cura nesses pacientes e como reproduzi-los de maneira mais segura.

A infectologista e pesquisadora australiana Sharon Lewin, uma das principais especialistas mundiais em cura do HIV, afirma que provavelmente vários mecanismos atuam ao mesmo tempo nos casos de transplante.

Segundo ela, novas abordagens que reforçam a resposta imunológica já conseguiram fazer alguns participantes de estudos controlar o vírus mesmo depois da suspensão dos antirretrovirais.

“Acho que a cura será possível sem transplante. Ensaios clínicos recentes com anticorpos e também com anti-PD-1 [tipo de imunoterapia que estimula a resposta do sistema imunológico] mostraram que, em alguns participantes, a imunidade natural específica contra o HIV pode ser reforçada o suficiente para permitir que eles controlem a replicação do vírus mesmo sem a terapia antirretroviral”, afirma Lewin.

Em 4 de março de 2019, Timothy Ray Brown foi fotografado em Seattle, nos Estados Unidos — Foto: Manuel Valdes/AP

Uma dessas tentativas ganhou atenção internacional justamente no Brasil.

Em um estudo liderado por Diaz, um paciente que vivia com HIV recebeu uma combinação de medicamentos e outras intervenções que buscavam atingir o reservatório e fortalecer a resposta do sistema imunológico.

Depois da interrupção dos antirretrovirais, ele ficou cerca de um ano em remissão , sem sinais detectáveis do vírus em exames. O HIV, porém, voltou posteriormente.

O caso ficou conhecido como “ paciente de São Paulo ”.

Para Diaz, o resultado chamou atenção porque o paciente chegou a apresentar características semelhantes às observadas em pessoas curadas por transplante , apesar de não ter passado pelo procedimento.

O caso, porém, também mostrou uma das dificuldades desse campo: um período sem vírus detectável não significa necessariamente que o HIV desapareceu do organismo. Pequenas quantidades podem permanecer escondidas e voltar a se multiplicar meses ou até anos depois.

Entre as estratégias em estudo, uma tenta “ acordar ” o HIV escondido para que as células infectadas possam ser eliminadas. Outra busca fazer o contrário: manter o vírus silenciado de forma permanente, mesmo sem os antirretrovirais.

Também são testados anticorpos, terapias celulares e edição genética. Na Unifesp , a equipe de Ricardo Diaz prepara um estudo de fase 2 com cerca de 60 voluntários para testar uma combinação de estratégias.

Nenhuma delas, até agora, resultou em uma cura segura e disponível para a população.

Mas os avanços no tratamento transformaram o HIV em uma condição controlável , e a prevenção também ganhou novas ferramentas, como a PrEP. A cura, porém, ainda exige estudos longos e acompanhamento por anos.

“A gente mostra os casos de sucesso, mas registra os casos que deram errado também. Não é uma coisa que é 100%. Todo esse processo científico é longo”, diz Diaz.

Hoje, a ciência já sabe que o HIV pode ser eliminado ou controlado por longos períodos sem medicamentos em casos raros.

O desafio é transformar esses resultados em uma estratégia segura, duradoura e acessível .

articles.title: Sou Manaus 2026: Léo Santana, Ana Castela e Filipe Ret agitam 3ª noite | G1
articles.standfirst: Mais de 100 mil pessoas circularam no sábado (5). O festival também apresentou espetáculos locais, reunindo ritmos do Norte do Brasil e manifestações da cultura de rua.
articles.summary: Com shows de Léo Santana e Ana Castela, o Sou Manaus 2026 reuniu milhares de pessoas e celebrou a cultura regional na terceira noite do festival no Centro Histórico.
articles.body:
Shows nacionais e regionais marcam terceira noite do Sou Manaus. — Foto: Jadson Lima/g1 AM

O Sou Manaus Passo a Paço 2026 teve, neste domingo (6), a terceira noite de programação no Centro Histórico de Manaus , com shows de artistas nacionais e apresentações de músicos e grupos locais. Filipe Ret, Léo Santana e Ana Castela estiveram entre as atrações da noite, que também reuniu dança, música regional, cultura urbana e outras manifestações culturais em diferentes espaços do festival.

O balanço parcial do evento foi divulgado pela Prefeitura de Manaus. Segundo estimativa da administração municipal, mais de 100 mil pessoas circularam pelo evento no sábado (5). Durante coletiva de imprensa, o prefeito Renato Júnior afirmou que a expectativa para a noite seguinte era de um público entre 30% e 40% maior.

No Palco Malcher, a programação começou com os DJs P1R4NH4S e seguiu com apresentações do amo do Boi Caprichoso Caetano Medeiros e o levantador de Toadas do Boi Garantido, David Assayag. O espaço também recebeu uma performance de dança da ArtFactory e o encontro entre a banda Tucumanus e o rapper manauara Victor Xamã.

A apresentação dos artistas locais reuniu diferentes sonoridades da música produzida no Norte do Brasil. O encontro marcou o retorno à cidade de um projeto que os artistas haviam apresentado recentemente no Festival João Rock, no interior de São Paulo.

Para Victor Xamã, voltar a cantar em Manaus ao lado de uma banda que acompanha há anos teve um significado especial. O artista destacou a importância de levar a produção cultural do Norte para outros espaços do país e defendeu mais oportunidades para profissionais de diferentes áreas da cultura na região.

“Eu sempre fico feliz de cantar para o meu povo, de cantar para a minha terra. E eu canto para que isso tudo mude, para que isso tudo melhore e para que a gente consiga mais oportunidades. Quando eu falo isso, não é só sobre a música, mas desde o jornalismo, cinema, moda e todas essas pontas que fazem a nossa cultura ser enxergada para o mundo inteiro”, afirmou.

O vocalista da Tucumanus, Clóvis Rodrigues, também destacou a oportunidade de apresentar em Manaus o mesmo espetáculo levado recentemente ao Sudeste. Segundo ele, a parceria permitiu mostrar parte da cultura e da produção artística amazonense para novos públicos.

Rapper Victor Xamã durante apresentação no Sou Manaus 2026 — Foto: Patrick Marques/g1 AM

“A gente está muito feliz porque conseguiu passar o recado, mostrar um pouco da nossa cultura e da nossa arte quando foi para o Sudeste. Agora, nada melhor do que voltar para a nossa terra com esse mesmo espetáculo e ter a oportunidade de estar em um festival tão grande quanto o Sou Manaus”, disse.

Segundo Clóvis, a apresentação também representou uma oportunidade de alcançar um público maior no festival. “É uma oportunidade muito massa de mostrar para a galera presente um pouco do nosso trabalho e da nossa história”, completou.

Depois das apresentações locais, o Palco Malcher recebeu Filipe Ret, Léo Santana e Ana Castela. Os shows fizeram parte da programação nacional da terceira noite, que também teve atrações distribuídas por outros espaços do Centro Histórico.

No Palco Alfândega, o público acompanhou apresentações de Dead Fish, Duquesa e Gloria Groove, além de DJs. Já o Palco Mangueirão recebeu Neto Barroncas, Tatá Jatobá, Luís Carlos, Gabriel Gonçalves, Tomi Xote e Banda Impakto.

Terceira noite do Sou Manaus tem shows de artistas locais e nacionais — Foto: Jadson Lima/g1 AM

A Casa da Cultura Urbana concentrou atividades voltadas à cultura urbana, com a Batalha de All Style, a Batalha Kidz, a Batalha de MCs e a Cypher de Break e All Style.

Público enfrenta calor e avalia programação

O calor de Manaus também fez parte da experiência de quem acompanhou a programação. A administradora Elaine Nascimento, que esteve no festival pela terceira vez, comentou sobre as altas temperaturas durante o evento e afirmou que, mesmo com o calor, aprovou a programação.

“Apesar desse calor estar derretendo a gente”, brincou Elaine.

Moradora de Manaus, ela afirmou que considera o Sou Manaus importante para a cultura e disse apoiar o evento. “Eu acredito que o Sou Manaus é um evento necessário para fortalecer a cultura. Acho supernecessário esse tipo de evento e eu apoio”, afirmou.

Manauaras recorrem a leques diante de calor no Sou Manaus — Foto: Jadson Lima/g1 AM

Elaine também avaliou que o festival pode passar por melhorias, mas disse não ter críticas negativas à edição.

Rosemeire Martins da Silva, de 50 anos, também acompanhou o evento com o marido e familiares. Ela contou que frequenta o festival todos os anos, mas avaliou que a programação desta edição teve mais atrações voltadas ao público jovem.

Segundo Rosemeire, algumas edições anteriores tiveram artistas que agradaram mais ao público da faixa etária dela. Apesar disso, ela afirmou que pretende retornar nesta segunda-feira (7) para acompanhar o show de Nathanzinho.

“Eu venho todos os anos com meu esposo e minha família. Os anos anteriores foram bons, mas este ano eu achei que não vieram muitos cantores bons como nos outros. A programação ficou mais voltada para os jovens e faltaram atrações para o nosso público”, afirmou.

Além dos shows, o festival movimentou as áreas de alimentação e os espaços ocupados por permissionários. Vendedores de comidas, bebidas, brinquedos e outros produtos participaram da estrutura montada para receber o público durante a programação.

O Sou Manaus Passo a Paço 2026 segue até 13 de setembro, com programação distribuída pelo Centro Histórico de Manaus.

articles.title: Clavicular’s controversial looksmaxxing empire comes under the microscope in explosive new study
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Looksmaxxing was once buried in obscure online communities where young men traded harsh judgments about appearance and extreme ideas about changing th.
articles.body: Looksmaxxing was once buried in obscure online communities where young men traded harsh judgments about appearance and extreme ideas about changing their bodies. A new study argues that figures such as Clavicular helped push that culture far beyond its original audience. The research maps a five-stage process showing how niche language, viral clips, controversy and mainstream coverage can turn an internet subculture into a recognizable part of popular culture.Clavicular and the rise of diagnostic masculinityThe study, authored by Dag Øivind Madsen of the University of South-Eastern Norway, uses livestreamer Braden Eric Peters, known online as Clavicular, as its central case study.Madsen describes a form of influence he calls “diagnostic masculinity.” Instead of simply showing followers an ideal lifestyle, these creators identify what they claim is wrong with their audience. Physical features become problems to measure, rank and correct, often with paid advice or products presented as solutions.That model fits naturally with looksmaxxing, a culture built around maximizing physical attractiveness. Some communities encourage ordinary grooming and fitness, but the more extreme corners promote dangerous practices and pseudo-medical claims.According to the study, Peters built his online identity around this insecurity. He reportedly sold a $50-a-month “Clavicular System,” while his broader streaming and coaching activities helped turn appearance-focused content into a lucrative business.The research traces the process through five stages: “vernacular incubation,” where communities develop their own language; “infrastructural assembly,” where creators build networks across platforms; “controversy acceleration”; “mainstream translation”; and finally “parodic consolidation.”That sequence helps explain why fringe internet ideas can suddenly appear everywhere. First, insiders create the culture. Then platforms give them distribution. Controversy supplies attention.How looksmaxxing moved from fringe forums to mainstream cultureClavicular’s rise illustrates how short-form video can change the reach of an online personality. Long livestreams can produce countless moments that other accounts then cut into short clips. Those clips require little context and can reach people who have never encountered the original community.Controversy can accelerate that process even further. Peters became associated with several highly publicized incidents, including a viral Cybertruck-related video, drug-related arrests and other episodes that attracted widespread online discussion. He was also hospitalized following an on-stream drug incident, according to the study’s account.Mainstream media then played another role. Peters appeared in interviews and television coverage where his unusual language and views were introduced to much larger audiences. Even critical reporting can have this effect because it gives unfamiliar online personalities a platform and explains their vocabulary to outsiders.The final stage is what Madsen calls “parodic consolidation.” Once terms such as “mogging” and “-maxxing” become familiar enough for jokes, the subculture has crossed an important cultural boundary. A Saturday Night Live sketch about looksmaxxing and Peters’ appearance at a Paris Fashion Week event offered striking examples of that transition.The study does not claim that every looksmaxxing community follows the same path. It examines one influencer and relies heavily on public digital traces, which can change quickly. It also does not measure whether mainstream viewers actually adopt the ideology behind the content.Still, the research offers a useful warning about how internet culture spreads. A fringe idea does not always need millions of devoted followers to become mainstream. Sometimes all it needs is a distinctive vocabulary, a controversial personality, a steady stream of viral clips and an audience willing to watch.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two engineers started a precision-equipment company from a Blackburn garage in 2021; five years later it was exporting to more than 70 countries
articles.summary: UK News: What began with two founders, a garage and a belief that unwanted technical equipment still had plenty of life left in it has become a remarkable inte.
articles.body: What began with two founders, a garage and a belief that unwanted technical equipment still had plenty of life left in it has become a remarkable international business story. In January 2021, Muhammad Geloo and Aziz Bham launched TT Instruments from the back of a vehicle inspection garage in Blackburn, Lancashire. They had no investors, no loans and no previous experience running a business. Their idea was simple, source high-value precision instruments that companies and laboratories no longer needed, restore them where necessary and give them a second life by selling them to customers who needed specialist equipment. Five years later, the small start-up had grown into a multi-million-pound business exporting to more than 70 countries across six continents. In 2026, that rapid international growth earned TT Instruments the King’s Award for Enterprise in International Trade.How two founders started TT Instruments from a garageTT Instruments began in January 2021 when Geloo and Bham started selling specialist test and measurement equipment from the back of a vehicle garage in Blackburn. According to The Lancashire Telegraph reporting on its King's Award, the founders had no external investors, loans or traditional business backing when they began. Instead, they saw an opportunity in equipment that large organisations were disposing of despite it still being valuable and functional. Their early operation was small, but the business model allowed them to connect unwanted precision equipment with engineers, researchers, universities and companies looking for specialist technology at lower prices. The founders initially sold equipment online, including through eBay, before rapidly expanding their stock and premises. Within months, the business had outgrown its original set-up and began moving towards a dedicated operation.The company gave high-value equipment a second lifeRather than manufacturing new instruments, TT Instruments built its business around reuse, refurbishment and resale. The company sources equipment from corporate disposal cycles and other organisations, then tests, restores and supplies it to customers around the world. Its inventory includes sophisticated technology such as Raman spectrometers, fibre-optic analysers, oscilloscopes and other electronic and scientific instruments. The approach has also given the business a circular-economy dimension because equipment that might otherwise be discarded can continue serving researchers and engineers. One example shared by founder Muhammad Geloo involved a Raman spectrometer restored in Blackburn that was subsequently used by a professor in South Korea for research into macular degeneration. The model allows customers to access specialist equipment while extending the useful life of expensive technology.Five years later, exports reached more than 70 countriesThe transformation from garage operation to international supplier happened remarkably quickly. By 2023, TT Instruments had moved into dedicated premises in Blackburn as its inventory expanded. The company says its exports reached more than 70 countries in a single year, with customers spread across six continents. International sales now account for roughly 75-80% of turnover, according to the company's King's Award information. Its customer base has included universities, small businesses and major technology companies, demonstrating how a specialist supplier from Lancashire managed to reach markets far beyond Britain. The company also achieved ISO 9001:2015 certification, strengthening its quality-management credentials. By its fifth year, TT Instruments had become a multi-million-pound enterprise with consistent year-on-year growth, a striking contrast to the tiny operation that began in a Blackburn garage in 2021.TT Instruments won the 2026 King's Award for International TradeThe company's rapid overseas expansion culminated in one of Britain's most prestigious business honours. In 2026, TT Instruments received the King's Award for Enterprise in International Trade, recognising its exceptional growth in international sales. The company says its export revenue more than doubled over the three-year assessment period, while overseas customers continued to represent the majority of its business. The Lancashire Telegraph reported that the enterprise had grown from its unusual garage beginnings into an international exporter. For Geloo and Bham, the award represents more than a business milestone; it validates a model built around giving specialist equipment a second life and making it accessible to customers around the world. What started with two founders and a modest garage operation has now become a global precision-equipment business.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Father of AI Geoffrey Hinton bets on Canada in tariff war with US; says, unlike America, Canada welcomes immigration; lead engineer lost H1-B visa
articles.summary: Tech News News: In the 1980s, Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton took an unconventional gamble, leaving a well-funded post at Carnegie Mellon Univ.
articles.body: In the 1980s, Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton took an unconventional gamble, leaving a well-funded post at Carnegie Mellon University to pursue an obscure, little-studied corner of machine learning at the University of Toronto. Four decades later, that foundational work has reshaped how modern artificial intelligence operates while transforming Canada’s largest metropolis into a powerhouse tech capital, CNN reported.While California has long reigned as the epicenter of global tech, an influential artificial intelligence ecosystem has emerged around Hinton in Ontario. “I was lucky because very few people were working on this 20 years ago, and so smart young students would come to Toronto … and they’ve now turned into a whole generation of AI leaders,” Hinton told CNN in an interview. Hinton added that, unlike the United States, under the Trump administration, Canada welcomes immigration, which technology companies have long relied on as a talent pipeline.Hinton’s proteges include Nick Frosst, who studied under Hinton before becoming one of his earliest hires at Google’s Toronto AI lab in 2017. Frosst later co-founded Cohere, an enterprise AI firm now valued at $7 billion. Rather than migrating south to build his venture, Frosst chose to stay put because of the city's diverse culture, which complements his dual life as a tech founder and frontman for the indie rock band Good Kid.Also, for Hinton, retaining domestic leadership in AI remains an urgent economic imperative. “I don’t think we can afford for Canada to get all this technology from the States or from China,” Hinton said, warning that if AI triggers widespread disruption, the wealth generated from automation must remain in Canada so it can be taxed locally to support displaced workers.What makes Toronto 'better than' many of the US 'tech cities'Toronto now reportedly boasts the world’s third best tech talent market, ahead of New York City but behind San Francisco and Seattle, according to an annual analysis by commercial real estate firm CBRE. This is also said to be thanks to educational institutions like the University of Toronto, and public-private research institutes like the Vector Institute, which Hinton co-founded.“There’s a great tech ecosystem, there’s also a great arts community, there’s also a great academic community, there’s a great business community,” Frosst told CNN, explaining that Toronto’s lack of a tech monoculture fosters independent thinking and innovation.Beyond cultural appeal, Canadian policy has proven to be a decisive advantage. Unlike past US administrations that restricted skilled immigration, Canada has positioned itself as an open haven for global engineers, providing crucial work permits when American H-1B visas fall through. Jordan Jacobs, managing partner at Radical Ventures, told CNN that these friendly policies attract talent adept at building for international audiences, aided by convenient short-haul flights to major American hubs like New York, Washington, and Chicago.Gennady Pekhimenko, who sold his startup CentML to Nvidia last year and now serves as senior director of AI software for the chip giant, said Toronto’s international food scene serves as a useful recruiting tool for out-of-town talent. He shared how one of Pekhimenko’s first hires at CentML was an Amazon engineer who was unable to renew his H1-B visa to stay in the United States. He could, however, get a Canadian work permit.One of Pekhimenko’s first hires at CentML was an Amazon engineer who was unable to renew his H1-B visa to stay in the United States. He could, however, get a Canadian work permit.Industry heavyweights have taken note. Giants like Google, Nvidia, Meta, and Microsoft now operate research outposts near the University of Toronto, flanked by startups and cross-sector players like pharmaceutical titan Sanofi, which committed nearly $300 million to a local AI center. The surge has propelled Toronto to the third-ranked tech talent market globally according to CBRE, trailing only San Francisco and Seattle.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Watch: CCTV captures moment Delhi's Satya Niketan building collapsed, leaving 6 dead
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: CCTV footage has captured the moment a multi-storey building collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area, killing six people and triggering a m.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CCTV footage has captured the moment a multi-storey building collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area, killing six people and triggering a major rescue operation.The building, which housed a boys' paying guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus, collapsed around 1.30 pm on Sunday while repair and construction work was underway. The death toll rose to six after one more person rescued during the night was declared dead.The CCTV footage showed the building suddenly giving way, sending debris crashing onto the road. Rescue and search operations continued through the night as teams searched the rubble for anyone who may still be trapped.Multiple agencies, including the Delhi Police, Delhi Fire Service, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and Delhi Disaster Management Authority, have been involved in the operation."One more person was rescued during the night but was brought dead, taking the toll to six," Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southwest) Amit Goel said, PTI reported.Police have registered a case against the building owner and others, while a magisterial inquiry has also been ordered. Officials are continuing efforts to trace people allegedly connected with the incident.To the residents, the collapse felt like a quake. “We felt the ground shake. When we ran outside, we saw that a house had completely collapsed,” said Roshan Pal, a student from Lucknow.“When I came out, a cloud of dust was spreading in all directions. That’s when we realised that the building had collapsed. We started removing one part of a wall soon after. Seven students were under it,” said Rahul Gaur, a resident, TOI reported.10 patients taken to Trauma CentreAccording to AIIMS, the JPN Apex Trauma Centre received 10 patients injured in the building collapse. Of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while another patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to injuries.Three patients have been admitted and are undergoing treatment. One of them underwent limb surgery, while another patient with minor injuries was discharged after observation.Investigators are examining whether construction work carried out in the basement may have contributed to the collapse.Initial inquiries suggested that the basement was prone to waterlogging, which may have weakened the structure. Investigators are now examining whether construction work aggravated the situation and contributed to the collapse.The MCD is also looking into the matter. Similar concerns over basement work, water accumulation and the structural condition of the building have emerged in the preliminary probe.Police are likely to examine whether permission had been obtained for the work and why construction was being carried out during the monsoon, sources said. "The building owner, contractor and labourers will be interrogated," an investigator said, TOI reported.It was not immediately clear whether the building owner had obtained permission for the construction or whether the work was being carried out illegally, allegedly in connivance with local authorities.MCD orders demolition of dangerous buildingAccording to the MCD, the premises of Building/House No. 13, Satya Niketan, New Delhi, was found to be in a "ruinous, dangerous condition" and posed a threat to people occupying, visiting or passing by the building as well as those in the neighbourhood.Under Section 348 of the DMC Act, 1957, read with Section 491 of the Act, the MCD has ordered the property to be demolished within three days of receipt of the order.The order said that if the owner fails to comply within the specified period, the MCD will demolish the building and recover the demolition charges as arrears of tax.The collapse has raised fresh questions over the safety of buildings being used as paying guest accommodations and the enforcement of construction and fire safety norms in densely populated areas of Delhi.Congress leader and AICC Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja questioned the BJP government over the safety of students living in such accommodations.“What is the BJP government doing? They have forgotten what happened at the coaching centre. A mafia is operating in Delhi. These children are sent away with so many hopes. They are the only support for their parents. Who is responsible for their safety?” Selja said.Former Delhi chief secretary Omesh Saigal said the incident should not be viewed in isolation and raised concerns over unauthorised construction in parts of the capital."Look at the kind of buildings constructed in Delhi—I would say that in some areas, one in five buildings is unauthorised; either the blueprints weren't approved, extra floors were added, or the construction is substandard," he said.Saigal also called for restrictions on new construction in areas that are already overcrowded. "At the very least, we should ban new construction in these areas. We must halt new construction or stop sanctioning building plans, for areas that are already over-congested and over-built. These are the things that need to be addressed," he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Homeopaths turn to allopathy amid job insecurity in Maharashtra, but just 10 have permission
articles.summary: The country's first medical council-registered homeopath, Mankhurd-based Neha Pawar, has kept her shop closed for the past year. In its place stands a.
articles.body: The country's first medical council-registered homeopath, Mankhurd-based Neha Pawar, has kept her shop closed for the past year. In its place stands a motor driving school. Pawar was given her certificate by the Maharashtra Medical Council (MMC) on Aug 3, despite severe pushback from the medical community.Maharashtra's total count of homeopaths allowed to practice modern medicine based on a one-year Certificate Course in Modern Pharmacology (CCMP) rose to ten this week, with Pawar and Mayuresh Kamble being the only two based in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. There are more than 10,000 such applicants. Experts point out that this massive demand to cross-practice stems from large-scale job insecurity.Dr Abhay Shukla, co-convener of Jan Swasthya Abhiyan, said, "We need to sympathise with them. They have years of training into something that does not work. Policies should now use whatever skills they have. The one-year pharmacology certificate course is insufficient but with rigorous training, they could be deployed in limited capacities at primary health centres."In Mankhurd's Ambedkar Nagar, Pawar's erstwhile clinic is surrounded by alternative practitioners like her. There is no MBBS doctor in sight, forcing locals to blindly trust whoever they can find. Those who do remember her recall her clinic as one of the many that opened and shut, but also a place they went to for occasional fever and cough check-ups.The area is home to many of the city's daily wage earners. Tasneem Usmani, a local pharmacist, said, "There is no option here for people. There are no MBBS doctors very close by, but others [alternative practitioners] are accessible and cheap, so they take a chance. The practitioners give their own tablets wrapped in paper."Pawar has been giving out allopathic medicines since 2017, years before she was legally permitted to do so. She told TOI that the shop is now closed for personal reasons and that she has no immediate plans to resume practice."All we check is if their registration is active with the homeopathic council and if they have any cases of negligence against them," said MMC registrar Dr Rakesh Waghmare.Her clinic was next to that of Shagufta Basha, a Unani practitioner, who said alternative medicine practitioners in the area -- such as herself, or ayurveda practitioners and homeopaths -- charge a small sum of Rs 100 and give out allopathic medicines to patients with fever, cough, typhoid and malaria. "TB patients are referred to a nearby BMC clinic. There is one MBBS doctor ten minutes away, but he is expensive for this population," she said.Dr Vijay Chavan, a pulmonologist who has treated TB patients for years in Mankhurd-Govandi, said the fees of an MBBS general physician there is Rs 200-300, so many walk into the first cheaper alternative they see, and it doesn't matter who sits there. "It is a risk and a problem, and it backfires many times with patients finally reaching doctors with some adverse reaction. But to be fair, even qualified MBBS doctors have been contributing to the haphazard use of medicines," Dr Chavan said.Inside homeopath Mayuresh Kamble's clinic at Survale Nagar, Badlapur (East), a rate card is pasted on the wall: Rs 150 for a consultation, Rs 200 for a consultation with an injection, Rs 50 for a BP check and the same charge for a dressing, Rs 100 for an injection prescribed by another doctor, and Rs 500-700 for a home visit.Most of his patients are working-class, he said. "When I started the practice here and had opened a shop in the area, there was almost nothing here. Buildings were coming up, and construction workers used to visit me for treatment."In the over an hour that TOI spent at his clinic, there were parents bringing their children with injuries for dressings, diabetes patients, respiratory distress patients, and patients complaining of fever and cough, many bringing their blood reports for advice, and even those with known high cholesterol.He looked at chest X-rays to check if one of his patients had TB or if it was a case of bronchitis. Many of his patients were people who had visited some other doctor in the recent past, farther from their homes, and landed up at his clinic because it was the closest option for a quick consultation.They also did not know that Kamble is a homeopath, though his board mentioned qualifications such as BHMS with CCMP. Homeopathy was almost entirely absent in his clinic. The medicines Kamble prescribed ranged from standard antibiotics to cough syrups, and he even considered statins for one of his patients if they did not visit a referred doctor. articles.summary: US News: An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into fl.
articles.body: An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames in a deadly crash that killed at least five people and injured five others.The Boeing 767-300, operating as Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 and operated by cargo carrier 21 Air, had arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when the aircraft ran off the runway shortly before 2pm local time.Dramatic footage showed the plane racing beyond the runway before crashing through an area used by warehouse workers and other businesses surrounding the airport. Thick black smoke and flames could be seen rising from the aircraft as emergency crews rushed to the scene.The plane eventually came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks. Images showed the aircraft largely intact but resting on its belly and engulfed in flames.Five people were killed in the crash, while another five were injured. Three of the injured were in critical condition, according to Miami-Dade County officials. It was initially unclear whether the pilots survived or whether all those killed were in vehicles struck by the aircraft.Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah said the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the cockpit following the crash, while some people were also trapped in vehicles. Crews had to rescue a person who was pinned beneath a vehicle.Huge emergency response as flights disruptedMore than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units and around 200 emergency personnel responded as firefighters battled an intense fire involving the aircraft. Specialised airport firefighting units used foam to extinguish the flames, while crews continued dealing with a fuel leak several hours after the crash.The accident brought operations at the busy airport to a halt for much of Sunday afternoon, with more than 160 flights cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late in the day. Some flights were also diverted to Orlando International Airport.The cause of the crash remains unknown and is being investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board, which sent a team led by its chairwoman, Jennifer Homendy, to Miami.Weather conditions may also form part of the investigation, with thunderstorms and wind gusts of up to 30 mph recorded in the area around the time of the crash.Aviation experts have raised questions about the aircraft's landing. Former United Airlines pilot Steve Arroyo said investigators would need to establish whether the plane touched down within the designated landing zone and, if not, why the crew did not abort the landing and attempt another approach.Former Transportation Department inspector general Mary Schiavo, meanwhile, said video of the landing appeared to show the aircraft floating above the runway for an extended period before touching down, potentially leaving insufficient runway to stop safely.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Far-right AfD makes historic breakthrough in Germany, wins 44% in state poll
articles.summary: Europe News: Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is poised for a historic breakthrough in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, opening the prospect of.
articles.body: Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is poised for a historic breakthrough in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, opening the prospect of the party seeking to govern despite falling short of an outright majority.With most interim results counted, the AfD was projected to secure a record 44% of the vote and far ahead of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which stood at 17%.Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s prominent leader in Saxony-Anhalt, described the result as “sensational” and said the party wanted to begin governing as soon as possible.According to the BBC report, a victory would mark an unprecedented development in post-war Germany, where no far-right party has previously taken control of a state government. State-level power would give the AfD influence over areas including policing, education and culture.Saxony-Anhalt, home to about 2.1 million people, has been a particular focus of concern because the state’s AfD branch is classified as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence service. Siegmund, 35, rejects the designation.Siegmund and the party’s national co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, celebrated as exit polls showed the AfD was on course to more than double its 2021 vote share.The AfD’s strong performance was quickly described by political opponents and commentators as a major turning point, highlighting the growing influence of the far-right party in German politics. Public broadcaster Das Erste even replaced its long-running crime drama Tatort with special coverage examining the significance of the result.“This isn’t just about Saxony-Anhalt,” Siegmund told supporters. “It’s a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal.”Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant.“This result is not just about Saxony-Anhalt,” Siegmund told supporters, calling it “a signal for the whole of Germany — a confident signal.”The result also drew attention abroad. US President Donald Trump shared a screenshot of the German election projection on his Truth Social platform, which Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev later reposted, describing the outcome as a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”.Dmitriev had previously praised the Russia-friendly party as one offering “hope and reason” and greater cooperation for Germany. US Vice-President JD Vance also backed the AfD ahead of Germany’s federal election last year, a move that drew criticism in Germany over alleged foreign political interference.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, however, offered a sharply contrasting reaction. The centre-right leader said that in Poland, “only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD.”Despite its strong performance, the AfD lacks the seats needed to govern alone, leaving Ulrich Siegmund facing a difficult path to power. He has so far ruled out leading a minority government, even as the party’s national leadership considers that option possible.Siegmund said the AfD would instead be willing to seek support from individual lawmakers or another party. “If necessary there’ll just be new elections, then we’d just get 50 or 55%,” he said.The outcome was also closely tied to the performance of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), whose ability to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament remained uncertain for several hours. Interim results eventually showed the party had crossed the threshold, meaning the AfD would not gain the additional seats it might otherwise have secured.The AfD was projected to win 39 of the 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament, leaving it three seats short of the 42 required for an outright majority.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesia cancelled all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport after the Anak Krakatau volcano erupted on Sunday, affecting thousan.
articles.body: Indonesia cancelled all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport after the Anak Krakatau volcano erupted on Sunday, affecting thousands of passengersFlight operations at domestic airports were also disrupted, stranding around 1,70,000 passengers as volcanic ash spread across parts of western Indonesia, BBC reported.According to Indonesia’s Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation, the eruption led to the spread of Volcanic ash across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province in Sumatra, prompting AirNav Indonesia to close airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as six other airports.Two ash clouds were identified by the country's volcanology agency and the Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre, using satellite imagery, with one rising to 6,100 meters that headed northeast over Jakarta, Banten, West Java and nearby waters. Another reached 15,200 meters and spread over parts of Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces.Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the government decided to temporarily shut additional airports after tests showed that volcanic ash had moved towards West Java.He called on airlines to speed up ticket refunds for passengers affected by cancellations and ensure that people with upcoming flights receive information promptly, helping prevent overcrowding at airports.Indonesia’s directorate general of civil aviation said it was monitoring the eruption’s effects on air travel and working with airlines, airport operators, air navigation service providers and the meteorology agency.“Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision,” Lukman F. Laisa, general of civil aviation, said in a statement.He cautioned that flight schedules could experience cascading disruptions as airlines seek to resume services, potentially affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity.The eruption also affected operations at Bali’s Gusti Ngurah Rai international airport and in Medan.Volcano remains activeLana Saria, head of Indonesia’s geological agency, said activity at Anak Krakatau has increased since July, with Sunday’s eruption being the strongest recorded during that period.She said the repeated eruptions suggest that magma and volcanic gases continue to be supplied from beneath the volcano, although officials cannot determine whether a larger eruption will take place.“We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” Saria said in a video briefing.According to Saria, the primary hazards include volcanic ash, high concentrations of gas, and the expulsion of hot rocks and other material near the crater.Anak Krakatau, meaning “child of Krakatau,” is the offspring of the famous Krakatau volcano, whose massive 1883 eruption led to a period of global cooling.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2010, Thailand sank 25 retired army tanks off Narathiwat to create artificial reefs; later research found 53 fish species thriving there
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2010, the Thai government carried out an unlikely piece of coastal engineering off Narathiwat province, sinking 25 retired army tanks, 273 disused .
articles.body: In 2010, the Thai government carried out an unlikely piece of coastal engineering off Narathiwat province, sinking 25 retired army tanks, 273 disused train carriages and 198 rubbish trucks into the southern Gulf of Thailand. The plan, backed by Thailand's queen, was meant to answer a request from local fishermen, who had watched stocks thin out after years of heavy fishing in the area. Rather than commission purpose-built reef structures, officials turned to hardware already sitting idle, using it to form the skeleton of 72 new reefs across the region. Years on, marine researchers returned to the site to see what had taken hold on the wreckage. Their survey, carried out across a cluster of tanks and a separate group of train wagons, set out to record which fish species had settled there and in what numbers, offering a detailed picture of how a reef assembled from military surplus develops over time.Why did Thailand sink retired tanks and train cars to build artificial reefsAccording to Al Jazeera, a news publication in Doha, the 2010 operation saw 25 abandoned army tanks, 273 old train carriages and 198 rubbish trucks placed in the sea as part of a wider plan to generate 72 new reefs across the region. The initiative was set in motion by Thailand's queen after fishermen in the country's restive southern provinces asked for assistance, having noticed a marked drop in fish stocks in waters they had long depended on.The choice of material was practical rather than symbolic. Large, hollow structures such as tanks and carriages provide instant shelter and surface area for marine organisms to colonise, without the cost of purpose-built reef modules. Al Jazeera described the deployment as "an unusual use of military hardware", noting that the vehicles were selected largely because they were already out of service and available in quantity.How many fish species did the artificial reefs attractA survey published in the Ramkhamhaeng International Journal of Science and Technology titled ‘First Insight on the Fish Species Composition at Two Artificial Reef Areas, Narathiwat Province, Thailand’, set out to document the fish community that had established itself on two sections of the site: a cluster of four tanks and a separate group of three train wagons. Researchers conducted a census at each structure, recording the abundance of every species present, before doing a further search to pick up any taxa missed in the initial count.The final tally came to 53 species across 21 families. Snappers were the most diverse group with seven species, followed by damselfishes and wrasses with four each. Neopomacentrus cyanomus, a small damselfish, was the dominant species in both the tanks and the wagons. According to the study, only the tanks supported large aggregations of fish, despite the wagons recording a marginally higher diversity score.Why did the tanks attract more fishAlthough the two structure types sit in the same stretch of water, they did not host identical assemblages. The tanks' more complex, enclosed shapes drew large numbers of small, cryptic and gregarious fish species that favour tight crevices and overhangs. This dominance of a few species is what pulled the tanks' overall diversity score down, even though more fish were visibly present.The train wagons, by contrast, offered less physical complexity but covered a wider footprint on the seabed. The study found that this larger occupied area attracted several species hovering in the surrounding water column, rather than sheltering directly within the structures themselves. The authors recorded a diversity index of 1.45 for the wagons, marginally ahead of the tanks, though the difference between the two areas was not statistically significant.How did the reefs support local fisheriesAmong the species recorded were groups with direct relevance to the fishing communities who originally requested the project. Snappers, the most species-rich family at the site, are a mainstay of commercial and small-scale fisheries throughout the Gulf of Thailand. Their consistent presence across both the tanks and the wagons points to the reef functioning as intended: a stable habitat capable of supporting economically important fish alongside the smaller reef species that dominate in numbers.The survey also noted the presence of the Humphead Parrotfish, an endangered species, among the taxa recorded at the site. According to the researchers, the artificial reefs of Narathiwat now hold "a typical reef fish community" that may serve as a shelter for such vulnerable species, in addition to the snappers and other groups of direct value to local fishing operations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Scottish clan kept a human skull for centuries because legend said removing it would bring ruin; now scientists are testing the story
articles.summary: US News: For generations, a human skull linked to a bloody Highland legend was kept within the Grant family, surrounded by a warning that taking it away could .
articles.body: For generations, a human skull linked to a bloody Highland legend was kept within the Grant family, surrounded by a warning that taking it away could spell disaster for the clan. Now, more than six centuries after the events at the heart of the story, forensic experts are examining the remains to find out whether the grisly relic really belongs to the medieval figure described in the legend. The investigation is being led by Grantown Museum in Scotland, which is preparing an exhibition and podcast titled The Legend of the Highland Skull. The museum says the project will explore a story involving forbidden love, powerful Highland clans, murder and a supposed curse.A skull, a castle and an old Highland legendThe story centres on what is now Castle Grant in Strathspey. According to the tradition recorded in an 1857 letter, the skull belonged to the head of Clan Comyn, who was allegedly killed during a violent struggle involving the Grants and MacGregors over the stronghold then known as Freuchie Castle.The Grants eventually made the castle their seat, and it became known as Castle Grant. The legend held that the skull was retained as a kind of grim family talisman but with one ominous condition: if it ever left Grant possession, the clan would supposedly lose its lands, influence and standing in Strathspey. That part of the story remains folklore rather than established history. What can be established is that a skull associated with the legend survived into modern times.The mysterious skull resurfaced in a boxThe relic disappeared from public view for years after the Grant family sold Castle Grant in 1983. It was eventually rediscovered by Lord Reidhaven, a descendant of the Grant chiefs, in a family storeroom. It was reportedly sitting inside a Harrods box alongside something almost as intriguing: a letter dating to 1857.The document had been written by Grigor Stuart, a minister from Kingussie who visited the Countess of Seafield at Castle Grant in October that year. His account described the skull and the story that had grown around it, including the claim that it was the remains of the last Comyn associated with Freuchie. Rather than allowing the mystery to remain a family story, Reidhaven brought the skull and letter to Dan Cottam, curator of Grantown Museum. That decision has now turned a centuries-old legend into a forensic investigation.What can science actually reveal?The skull is being examined by specialists in human remains and osteology, including Cat Irving, a human-remains conservator associated with Surgeons’ Hall Museums in Edinburgh. The first examination has already raised fresh questions. The skull appears to have been deliberately sawn across the forehead, with a metal hinge and hook attached to it, effectively turning part of the skull into a container.Researchers are working to establish basic facts that could either support or challenge the traditional account, including whether the remains belonged to a man or woman, the person’s approximate age, and any evidence of injury or disease. Most importantly, determining the skull’s age and comparing the physical evidence with the historical account will be crucial to assessing whether the story holds up.The curse is being tested against historyThe timing is particularly striking. The skull has now left the possession of the Grant family, precisely the act the legend warned would bring about the clan’s downfall. But this time, the purpose is not to test the curse.Grantown Museum is using the investigation to examine how stories survive, change and acquire authority as they pass from one generation to another. The project combines historical research, forensic examination and storytelling rather than treating the supernatural element as established fact.The museum’s Legend of the Highland Skull project includes a four-part podcast, an animated short film and an exhibition. The exhibition is scheduled to run at Grantown Museum from September 7 to October 31, 2026, while the podcast began releasing episodes in September. And after roughly 600 years of legend, one question finally has a chance of being answered: whose skull is it really?Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Satya Niketan exposes a hard truth: Students come to Delhi to build their futures, but live in unsafe buildings
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The collapse of a five-storey boys’ PG in Satya Niketan on Sunday has brought back a question Delhi has repeatedly failed to answer: how sa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The collapse of a five-storey boys’ PG in Satya Niketan on Sunday has brought back a question Delhi has repeatedly failed to answer: how safe are the buildings in which thousands of students live? The building, close to Delhi University’s South Campus, was being used as paying-guest accommodation and had a basement and five upper floors. Repair work was reportedly being carried out in the basement when the structure came down around 1.30pm. By evening, five people had died and several others had been pulled out of the rubble, while rescue teams continued to search for those who could still be trapped.Delhi’s student colonies have grown faster than regulationSatya Niketan is hardly an exception. Delhi has dozens of neighbourhoods that have gradually turned into student colonies, driven by the city’s universities, coaching centres and private institutes. Katwaria Sarai, Saket, Munirka, Ber Sarai, Mukherjee Nagar, Malviya Nagar, Kamla Nagar, Kingsway Camp, Model Town and Roop Nagar etc. are packed with students during the academic year and have developed similar ecosystems. Satya Niketan is part of this larger story.The problem is not simply a shortage of roomsNo government can provide accommodation to every student or aspirant who comes to Delhi. Nor can every family afford university hostels or purpose-built private accommodation. But a shortage of affordable housing cannot become a justification for unsafe buildings. In several student hubs, every square foot of a property can have commercial value. Buildings are divided into smaller rooms, additional occupants are accommodated and spaces such as basements and terraces can acquire uses for which they may never have been designed.The problem becomes particularly serious when old buildings undergo repeated alterations without proper structural assessment. A basement may be modified, walls may be removed, additional floors or rooms may be added and electrical or plumbing systems may be stretched to cope with a much larger population. In Satya Niketan, repair work in the basement at the time of the collapse will naturally be examined as part of the investigation. But the precise cause must come from a proper structural inquiry, not from assumptions made in the immediate aftermath of a tragedy.Delhi has already seen the warning signsThe capital does not have to look far for reminders of what can happen when regulation comes after disaster instead of before it. In July 2024, three civil services aspirants died after the basement of a coaching centre in Old Rajinder Nagar was flooded. The tragedy triggered inspections, sealing drives and a nationwide debate over the safety of coaching hubs. Yet nearly two years later, questions about compliance and enforcement in the area have not disappeared. The CBI has also alleged lapses by three junior MCD officials in the discharge of their duties.Then came the building collapse in Saidulajab near Saket in May this year. Six people died, including five young medical and engineering graduates. The tragedy again turned the spotlight on unauthorised construction. Police had reportedly flagged illegal construction at the four-storey building before its collapse. Following the incident, MCD launched action in the area, while officials said notices had been issued to hundreds of potentially illegal structures in the wider Mehrauli-Chhattarpur belt. The familiar pattern was repeated: tragedy, scrutiny and enforcement.The numbers raise another uncomfortable questionThe scale of enforcement action itself shows how widespread the problem can be. After a series of deadly incidents in June, MCD said 82 properties had been demolished and another 43 sealed during a citywide drive against illegal and unauthorised structures. The numbers are significant, but they also leave Delhi with a much more difficult question. How many buildings are being occupied today that have never been properly inspected? And how many violations are visible to residents, landlords and local officials but remain unaddressed until something goes wrong?A July 2026 report of the Supreme Court-constituted Monitoring Committee also highlighted non-compliance with fire-safety norms involving residential properties being used for mixed or commercial purposes. This is important in the context of student neighbourhoods, where residential buildings can gradually become high-density accommodation or commercial premises. The issue is therefore not merely whether a building has a valid address or whether rent is being paid. It is whether the building is being used in a manner consistent with its structural, fire and occupancy requirements.Students should not have to choose between education and safetyFor a young person arriving in Delhi, a PG is rarely a matter of lifestyle. It is often the most practical way to stay close to a university or coaching centre while keeping costs under control. A student and their parents may compare rent, distance, food and basic facilities, but they cannot reasonably be expected to judge whether a basement alteration has compromised a building or whether a five-storey structure is carrying more occupants than it was designed to support. That responsibility lies with the regulatory system.Delhi therefore needs a system that works before a building collapses. Student-heavy neighbourhoods should be mapped and buildings being used as PGs and hostels should face periodic structural and fire-safety checks. Occupancy limits must mean something. Unauthorised construction and basement conversions cannot be overlooked simply because there is strong demand for rooms. Open drains, narrow access lanes, blocked exits and ageing structures may look like routine inconveniences on an ordinary day, but during an emergency they can become matters of life and death.Satya Niketan cannot become another forgotten warningThe danger now is that Satya Niketan will follow the familiar script: an inquiry will be ordered, responsibility will be debated, notices will be issued and attention will eventually move elsewhere. Delhi has already been through this cycle after Old Rajinder Nagar and Saidulajab. Yet students continue to arrive, landlords continue to rent out rooms and neighbourhoods continue to become more crowded.Students come to Delhi to prepare for exams, attend college, start careers and build a future. They should not have to calculate the risk of the building in which they sleep. Satya Niketan has exposed a hard truth that the capital can no longer afford to ignore: Delhi’s student-housing problem is not only about affordability or availability. It is about safety, accountability and regulation. And the question after yet another collapse is painfully simple — how many more students have to die before the city treats safe student housing as a basic requirement rather than an afterthought?You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news.
